  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
At seventy-seven, Mrs. Amara Osei had spent decades navigating the brutal compromises of power. As a veteran politician in a large Midwestern city, she had long prided herself on her composure, her ability to read a room and command a stage. But the composure she wore like armor had begun to crack in the months since a quiet, shameful night that no one in her party or her family knew about. The night her husband of forty-two years, a retired professor with a gentle public demeanor, had struck her for the first time.

The argument had been trivial—something about a misplaced donation letter—but the escalation had been swift and terrifying. He had not shouted. He had simply stood, walked over to where she sat at the kitchen table, and backhanded her across the mouth. She remembered the shock more than the pain: the bright, wet taste of blood, the sight of her own blood spotting the white sleeve of her blouse. She remembered sitting there, frozen, while he calmly returned to his chair and resumed reading the newspaper. What she could not remember, no matter how hard she tried, was what happened in the hour that followed. The memory was an incomplete picture, a photograph torn in half. She would feel the guilt wash over her—a hot, suffocating wave—whenever she tried to piece it together, and then she would shove the whole thing away before she could reach the missing part. It was easier not to know.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel dangerous in ways it never had before. At city council meetings, when a colleague raised his voice in debate—even a controlled, professional tone of disagreement—her stomach would clench and her palms would go cold. She had learned to watch the faces of men, to measure the distance between their bodies and hers. Proximity itself had become a threat. She found herself sitting at the far end of the conference table, her back to the wall, scanning the door. At night, she could not sleep unless every light in the house was on, and even then she would lie awake listening for footsteps. She had taken to checking behind her as she walked from the parking garage to the office, a habit that made her feel foolish and old.

Her husband had apologized, of course. He had wept, promised it would never happen again, and she had accepted his apology because that was what she did. But the mistrust had rooted itself deep in her chest. She found herself watching his hands when he reached for a glass, noting the way he cleared his throat. She had come to believe that she was permanently changed, that something essential in her had been broken and could not be repaired. The emotions she used to feel—joy at a policy win, pride in a speech, warmth at a grandchild’s visit—felt inaccessible, as though they belonged to a stranger. She was certain she would never feel normal again.

The avoidance crept into her life quietly. She stopped attending evening fundraisers because the drive home in the dark felt unbearable. She stopped inviting her husband to public events, inventing excuses about scheduling conflicts. Her staff noticed she was shorter with them, more guarded. She began delegating the more contentious committee work, telling herself she was mentoring younger colleagues. In truth, she was avoiding any room where a voice might rise.

What finally brought her to a therapist’s office was not the fear or the sleeplessness. It was the startle response. At a ribbon-cutting ceremony last month, a child had popped a balloon near her elbow. She had screamed—a raw, undignified sound—and had to excuse herself to the restroom to stop shaking. The mayor had looked at her with concern. Her colleagues had exchanged glances. She knew, with a cold certainty, that her career could not survive another such moment. She needed the old Amara back, the one who could stand in any room and feel unshakeable. She was not sure that woman still existed, but she was terrified enough to look.
